name: Memory in the Age of AI Agents (Hu et al.)
venue: arXiv preprint, arXiv:2512.13564 [cs.CL] (also cs.AI). v1 submitted 2025-12-15; v2 revised 2026-01-13. CoRR/DBLP record DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2512-13564. Not peer-reviewed at time of writing (preprint).

code_url: N/A (a survey; no method code). Curated paper-list repository is maintained instead (see maintained_repo_url).
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/Shichun-Liu/Agent-Memory-Paper-List (official 'Agent-Memory-Paper-List', ~2.1k stars, MIT license; organizes papers by the forms x functions x dynamics taxonomy under Factual / Experiential / Working Memory each split into Token-level / Parametric / Latent; last major commit 2026-03-03, README updated through 2026-02-10).
task_domain: Survey/taxonomy of memory for foundation-model-based (LLM) agents, spanning conversation/long-term dialogue, personalization, multi-source/multi-hop QA, deep research, web navigation, desktop/mobile GUI agents, embodied/game environments, code/software engineering, recommendation, role-playing, and multi-agent systems (an anchor agent-memory survey, not a single-task method).
problem_setting: An up-to-date, comprehensive survey aiming to de-fragment the rapidly expanding agent-memory field. It first delineates the SCOPE of agent memory and explicitly distinguishes it from LLM memory, RAG, and context engineering, then organizes the literature through the unified 'Forms-Functions-Dynamics' triangle. Settings covered are predominantly interactive, multi-turn, long-horizon agent-environment loops (single- and multi-agent), where memory enables long-horizon reasoning, continual adaptation, personalization, and self-evolution. It formalizes a memory state M_t updated by three lifecycle operators Formation F, Evolution E, Retrieval R within the agent loop (policy a_t = pi(o_t, m_t, Q)). The survey proposes no new method, dataset, or experiments; it offers a unified conceptual framework, a benchmark/framework compilation (Tables 8-9), and a forward-looking positions/frontiers section.
what_is_retrieved: Across surveyed systems: factual knowledge (dialogue facts, user profiles, KG triples, documents), experiential traces (raw trajectories, reflections, distilled insights/workflows/rule-templates, procedural skills), and working-memory content (active context, intermediate states, tool outputs, summaries). The survey frames retrieval (operator R) as returning a context-dependent memory signal m_t for the LLM policy.
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID / primarily GROWING memory. The survey's defining position is that agent memory is a persistent, evolving store the agent writes and updates over multi-turn, multi-task interaction (vs RAG's static external corpus for single-task invocation). It explicitly notes graph-based agent memory 'constructs, extends, or reorganizes' itself throughout operation, treating the store as a 'living, evolving representation of experience'; static external knowledge (docs/KB) is covered but framed as the RAG boundary case.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Survey-level: reviewed retrieval predominantly uses fixed top-k similarity (semantic retrieval is called 'the default choice in most agentic memory frameworks'), but the survey explicitly critiques 'forced top-K retrieval' as a source of noise/spurious recall and reviews dynamic retrieval policies, reranking, and hybrid schemes. It does not advocate a single completeness-vs-top-k objective; both relevance-driven top-k and comprehensive 'retrieve from all stores' designs (e.g., MIRIX) are surveyed. [uncertain] as a single normative stance.
cbr_cycle_coverage: N/A (a survey, not a CBR method). The surveyed lifecycle (Formation / Evolution / Retrieval) plus experiential reuse maps loosely onto CBR Retain/Revise/Retrieve/Reuse, but the survey does not use CBR phase terminology.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False - the survey frames memory via cognitive science (declarative memory: episodic vs semantic; multicomponent / embedded-processes working-memory models) and its own forms/functions/dynamics taxonomy. It does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner.
retrieval_unit: Survey taxonomy of memory units rather than one unit. By FORM: token-level discrete units (chunks, dialogue logs, experience pools, tree/graph nodes, KG triples/subgraphs, hierarchical pyramids), parametric units (weight edits, adapters/LoRA modules), latent units (KV-cache, soft/continuous memory tokens, hidden states). By FUNCTION: factual entries (facts, profiles, documents), experiential entries (trajectories, reflections, workflows, rules, skills), working-memory entries (active context, intermediate states). Retrieved 'reading' units span snippet / dialogue segment / full trajectory / distilled insight / KG-subgraph / document / latent token.
index_source: Hybrid construction. The store is primarily a GROWING memory written/evolved online during multi-turn, multi-task interaction (formation + evolution operators), optionally seeded with cross-trial information distilled from prior trajectories; static external knowledge (RAG-style corpora) is covered as the boundary case. Short-term vs long-term memory phenomena are framed as emerging from temporal invocation patterns of F/E/R rather than fixed modules.
index_structure_topology: Survey taxonomizes token-level topology by complexity/dimensionality: Flat (1D: chunk sets, dialogue logs, experience pools), Planar (2D: single-layer Tree or Graph structures), and Hierarchical (3D: Pyramids and Multi-layer graphs for vertical abstraction). Concrete topologies reviewed: flat vector stores, knowledge/temporal-knowledge graphs (Zep, AriGraph, HippoRAG, EMG-RAG, G-Memory three-tier hierarchy), structured profiles/relational DBs, hierarchical OS-style memory (MemGPT main/external; MemoryOS S/M/LTM), and tree/community-graph indices (GraphRAG). Parametric and latent forms have their own (non-index) organizations.
retriever_type: Survey-level taxonomy of retrieval strategies: Lexical (TF-IDF, BM25), Semantic/dense (Sentence-BERT, CLIP; 'default choice in most agentic memory frameworks'), Graph retrieval (node/triple seeding + K-hop ego-graph expansion, personalized PageRank in HippoRAG, LLM-steered subgraph exploration, temporal-graph retrieval), Generative retrieval (DSI/tool-as-token; noted as under-explored in agent memory), and Hybrid (lexical+semantic, e.g., Agent KB, MIRIX; multi-factor scoring as in Generative Agents' recency/importance/relevance). No single canonical retriever is proposed.
retriever_learning_signal: Survey-level: most reviewed retrieval is off-the-shelf (lexical/dense similarity, heuristic recency/importance/relevance scoring). Trainable/learned variants are surveyed: Rewrite-Retrieve-Read trains a small RL rewriter; the survey's Frontiers section (RL integration) charts a progression from RL-free heuristic/prompt pipelines, to partially RL-involved designs governing selected memory operations (e.g., Memory-R1, MemSearcher, MemAgent, Mem-alpha), to envisioned fully RL-driven memory where architectures and control policies are learned end-to-end. The survey itself proposes no learned retriever.
query_construction: Survey-level: query construction is treated as a 'translation layer' between the user's surface utterance and the memory index, via (a) direct raw-query retrieval (simple baseline), (b) Query Decomposition into sub-queries (Visconde, ChemAgent; planner-driven in PRIME/MA-RAG; failure-aware fine-grained sub-queries in Agent KB), and (c) Query Rewriting / hypothetical-document generation (HyDE; MemoRAG conditions on compressed global memory; MemGuide produces command-like intent phrases; ToC tree-of-clarifications; RL-trained rewriter).
query_granularity: Survey-level: spans task-level (one-shot retrieval at t=0), step/state-level (intermittent or continuous retrieval on contextual triggers during reasoning), and decomposed sub-query level (multiple sub-queries per task). The survey formalizes this with a piecewise retrieval schedule and does not standardize a single granularity.
when_to_retrieve: Survey-level: ranges from always-on retrieval (e.g., MIRIX retrieves from all six memory stores per query) to selectively/agent-triggered retrieval. The survey's 'Retrieval Timing and Intent' section reviews one-shot (t=0 only), intermittent/continuous, and adaptive (model- or controller-decided) triggering; no single policy is prescribed.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Survey-level taxonomy under 'Automated Retrieval Timing and Intent': (a) LLM/controller-decided from the query alone (MemGPT, MemTool invoke retrieval functions OS-style), (b) fast-slow / cognitive-state-aware triggering that integrates the model's evolving reasoning state (to fix the limitation of query-only static judgments), and (c) automated retrieval INTENT selecting WHICH store to access (AgentRR switches between low-level procedural templates and high-level experiential abstractions on environmental feedback). The survey warns of a 'silent failure mode' when the agent over-trusts internal knowledge and fails to trigger retrieval, causing hallucination.
reranking: Survey-level: reranking is identified as one of the four phases of the retrieval pipeline (Post-Retrieval Processing: re-ranking, filtering, aggregation) and as a key lever in modular RAG and in mitigating semantic-drift/forced-top-K noise. Multi-factor scoring (recency+importance+relevance in Generative Agents; mixed-utility in MAICC) and two-stage graph reranking (semantic node retrieval then topology expansion) are surveyed. No single reranker is proposed.
retrieved_context_refinement: Survey-level: Post-Retrieval Processing is an explicit pipeline phase covering re-ranking, filtering (distractor/noise suppression, token pruning, importance-based selection), and aggregation of decomposed sub-query results; compression/summarization and reason-in-documents-style draft generation (MemoRAG) are also covered. Refinement is framed as filtering noise while providing essential information 'at the right moments.'
tool_document_engineering: N/A (memory survey; tool/skill-description engineering is largely out of scope, though tool-use experience, ToolMem learnable tool-capability memory, and tool-output memory are mentioned as experiential memory and as memory-relevant signals in tool benchmarks like ToolBench).
index_content_separation: Covered: OS/virtual-context memory separates a small active/working context from a larger external store paged on demand (MemGPT main vs external context; MemoryOS short/mid/long-term; MemOS tree memory + memcube). Hierarchical/pyramid forms keep detailed traces for the active subgoal while compressing completed subgoals into higher-level summaries that are selectively retrieved (HAgent, ILM-TR). Treated as a forms/working-memory pattern rather than a formal index-vs-content principle.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Partially: the survey discusses living/evolving graph memory that is constructed, extended, or reorganized during operation, and notes context engineering's standardization of communication protocols such as MCP for tool calls; it does not center a formal static-vs-live tool-index CRUD-sync mechanism (that is the tool-retrieval survey's domain). [uncertain] as a first-class agent-memory axis here.
tool_dependency_awareness: N/A (inter-tool dependency modeling is out of scope for this memory survey).
how_retrieved_used: Survey-level: retrieved memory signal m_t is formatted for direct consumption by the LLM policy (prompt augmentation as textual snippets or structured summary), and across forms is also used as latent-token injection (latent memory interfering with/augmenting the forward pass; KV-cache reuse), parametric internalization (weight edits/adapters as implicit memory), experiential reuse (workflows/skills/rules guiding new tasks), and training signal (RL-optimized memory control in the frontiers section).
planning_integration: Survey-level: memory supplies context for planning/acting at varied points - one-shot at task initialization, intermittent/continuous per-step retrieval, planner-agent-driven global retrieval plans before sub-query decomposition (PRIME, MA-RAG inspired by ReAct), subgoal-level hierarchical working memory (HAgent), and beam-search planning over KG memory (D-SMART). The survey abstracts this via the agent loop a_t = pi(o_t, m_t, Q) with flexible memory-agent coupling rather than one integration scheme.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Survey-level: spans per-answer (single retrieval at t=0), per-step/per-turn (intermittent or continuous retrieval triggered by contextual/cognitive state), per-sub-query (decomposed retrieval-then-aggregate), and iterative refinement loops (ILM-TR inner loop until evidence/answer stabilize). Not standardized to one granularity.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (a survey, not a CBR adaptation method). The closest analogues surveyed are Evolution-operator mechanisms (consolidation, conflict resolution, refinement) and experiential abstraction of trajectories into reflections/workflows/rules, plus RL-driven memory updating.
retrieved_item_representation: Survey-level: organized by FORM into Token-level (explicit, discrete, human-readable text: raw dialogue, summaries, reflections, workflows, rule-templates, KG triples, executable skills), Parametric (information encoded into model weights via fine-tuning, model editing, or attached adapters/LoRA - implicit), and Latent (hidden-state / soft continuous memory tokens / KV-cache - operating in the model's internal representational space). Surface forms thus range from raw trajectory to distilled strategy/workflow to executable program/skill to latent soft tokens.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Survey-level spectrum, explicitly highlighted: raw observations/dialogue at the lowest level; distilled reflections/insights and high-level 'thought-templates', universal workflows, and rule templates (e.g., Reflexion's self-reflection long-term memory; AWM workflows); procedural skills; and structured semantic/relational abstractions (KG world models, hierarchical schemata). The survey frames a progressive raw -> abstracted continuum, especially for experiential memory.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Survey-level: noise robustness is addressed via Post-Retrieval Processing (filtering distractors, token pruning, importance-based selection, reranking), external evaluators that filter redundant/inconclusive content during summarization (convolutional consistency discriminator; DeBERTa filtering), conflict resolution and consolidation in the Evolution operator, online LLM filtering (HippoRAG 2), and balancing retrieval timing to avoid both knowledge gaps (silent-failure hallucination) and excessive-retrieval noise. RL-trained summarization (PPO/GRPO in Mem1, MemAgent) is also surveyed.
memory_type: Survey/taxonomy covering all listed types via the FORM x FUNCTION matrix. Functions: Factual (knowledge/facts/profiles ~ semantic), Experiential (insights, workflows, skills, reflections ~ episodic+procedural), and Working memory (active context management). Forms: Token-level (episodic/skill-library/workflow/graph realizations), Parametric, and Latent. It deliberately moves beyond the coarse long/short-term temporal split.
write_back: True (survey-level) - the Formation operator (F: M_t, phi_t -> M^form) creates new memory artifacts and the Evolution operator (E) integrates/consolidates them; write-back of facts, experiences, profiles, workflows, and skills is central across surveyed systems (Mem0, MemGPT, A-MEM, Reflexion/ExpeL, AWM, ReasoningBank, etc.).
online_growth: Yes (survey-level) - a defining property distinguishing agent memory from single-task RAG: memory grows and is reorganized online during multi-turn, multi-task deployment (long-term memory updated episodically at task boundaries or continuously throughout operation). Graph memory is explicitly described as a 'living, evolving representation of experience.'
write_back_trigger: Survey-level taxonomy: per-step accumulation (minimal logging M_{t+1} = M_t U {o_t}), at task boundaries (episodic long-term updates), reflective/self-critique writing (Reflexion, reflection mechanisms), incremental semantic summarization (chunk-by-chunk fusion in MemGPT/Mem0; RL-enhanced in Mem1/MemAgent), and learned/RL-governed memory construction (Memory-R1, Mem-alpha). No single trigger is prescribed; the survey notes triggers range from always-on to selectively/agent-decided.
failure_experience_usage: Survey-level: experiential memory explicitly abstracts 'procedural knowledge from past successes AND failures'; failure-driven mechanisms are surveyed (e.g., Agent KB's teacher model observing the student's failures to generate corrective fine-grained sub-queries; reflection on failed trials in Reflexion/Retroformer; hindsight reflection). Both success and failure experiences are treated as reusable, not success-only.
memory_evolution_update: Survey-level: a dedicated 'Memory Evolution' taxonomy with three branches - (a) Consolidation (local consolidation, cluster fusion, global integration; incremental semantic summarization), (b) Updating (external-DB conflict resolution: rule-based replace/delete -> temporally-aware soft deletion/invalid-timestamps in Zep -> delayed-consistency -> fully learned update policies; plus internal parametric updates), and (c) Forgetting (pruning by time expiration, low access frequency, low informational value; soft weight decay e.g. MAICC; stochastic token replacement). Goes well beyond append-only to dedup-merge, conflict-resolve, soft/decay-forget, and refine-overwrite.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: Survey-level: increasingly yes, and the survey dedicates a Frontiers subsection to it. It charts RL-free heuristic/prompt pipelines -> partially RL-involved designs governing selected memory operations (retrieval/construction/management as RL-optimized, e.g., Memory-R1, MemSearcher, Mem-alpha, RL-trained Rewrite-Retrieve-Read; Mem1/MemAgent for summarization) -> envisioned fully RL-driven, model-native self-optimizing memory. The survey positions fully-RL-driven memory as 'the next major stage.' Most current systems still use fixed similarity top-k, however.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: Survey-level: explicitly covered. Multi-agent memory is a Frontiers topic; surveyed shared-memory mechanisms include Memory Sharing (centralized repository of past queries/responses for asynchronous reuse across agents), G-Memory (three-tier insight/query/interaction graph hierarchy for multi-agent systems), MIRIX (multi-agent memory system), LEGOMem (modular procedural memory for multi-agent workflow automation), and RCR-Router (role-aware context routing with structured shared memory). Both single-agent private and cross-agent shared memory are taxonomized.
benchmarks: No new benchmark is introduced. The survey compiles two categories (Table 8): (1) memory/lifelong/self-evolving-oriented: MemBench, MemoryAgentBench, LoCoMo, WebChoreArena, MT-Mind2Web, PersonaMem, LongMemEval, PerLTQA, MemoryBank, MPR, PrefEval, LOCCO, StoryBench, MemoryBench, Madial-Bench, Evo-Memory, LifelongAgentBench, StreamBench, DialSim, LongBench / LongBench v2, RULER, BABILong, MM-Needle, HaluMem, HotpotQA; (2) other agent-oriented but memory-relevant: ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, AgentGym, BabyAI, WebShop, WebArena, MMInA, ToolBench. Also references GAIA, XBench, BrowseComp, SWE-bench Verified, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue in the RAG-vs-memory discussion.
benchmark_family: memory (agent-memory / lifelong-learning / self-evolving evaluation survey). Sub-families spanned: memory (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, MemoryBank, MemBench, PerLTQA, PersonaMem, HaluMem), long-context (LongBench/v2, RULER, BABILong, MM-Needle), multi-hop/QA (HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue), web (MT-Mind2Web, WebChoreArena, WebShop, WebArena, MMInA, Online-Mind2Web-style), embodied/game (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, BabyAI, StoryBench), tool (ToolBench), code (SWE-bench Verified), deep-research (GAIA, XBench, BrowseComp), and lifelong/streaming (StreamBench, LifelongAgentBench, MemoryBench, Evo-Memory).
baselines: N/A - a survey with no experiments. It instead tabulates and compares representative memory systems (e.g., MemGPT, Mem0, A-MEM, Zep, HippoRAG/HippoRAG 2, GraphRAG, AriGraph, EMG-RAG, G-Memory, Memory-R1, MIRIX, MemoryOS, MemOS, Reflexion, ExpeL, AWM, ReasoningBank, Memento, Memp, MemGen, MEM1, MemAgent) along forms/functions/dynamics axes (Tables 1, 8, 9).
key_metrics: Survey-level: no single metric is proposed; it surveys metrics used across benchmarks - QA/dialogue accuracy and F1, memory recall/reference accuracy, retrieval precision/recall, task success/pass rate (web/embodied/code, e.g., SWE-bench Verified resolved %), long-context retrieval accuracy, lifelong-learning measures (catastrophic forgetting, forward/backward transfer, test-time adaptation), hallucination metrics (HaluMem), and efficiency/cost (token budget, latency). It emphasizes precision and recall in retrieval plus continual-learning transfer metrics.
headline_result: N/A (no empirical headline number; it is a survey). Its headline contribution is the unified 'Forms (token-level / parametric / latent) x Functions (factual / experiential / working) x Dynamics (formation / evolution / retrieval)' taxonomy, plus a clear conceptual delineation of agent memory from LLM memory, RAG, and context engineering, and compilations of memory benchmarks (Table 8) and open-source frameworks (Table 9). It was Hugging Face Daily Paper #1 (2025-12-16).
ablations: N/A (no experiments/ablations). The survey's comparative tables (Table 1 token-level methods by 1D/2D/3D topology and factual/experiential/working type; Table 8 benchmarks; Table 9 open-source frameworks) and lifecycle formalization (F/E/R) function as the structured cross-system comparison clarifying which design choices each system adopts.
evaluation_decoupling: Conceptually yes - the survey distinguishes isolated memory-retrieval evaluation (intrinsic: retrieval precision/recall, reference/memory accuracy, hallucination) from end-to-end lifelong/agentic task performance, and explicitly separates benchmarks 'explicitly designed for memory' from 'other benchmarks that implicitly stress memory through long-horizon interaction.' It notes lifelong benchmarks track performance on current AND previously seen tasks (decoupling retention from immediate task success). The survey itself reports no numbers.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both, as a taxonomy: outcome metrics via end-to-end task success across web/embodied/code/QA benchmarks; process/intermediate metrics via memory reference accuracy, retrieval precision/recall, memory hallucination (HaluMem), forgetting/transfer measures, and trajectory/consistency quality. The survey advocates measuring intermediate memory quality and continual-learning dynamics, not only final outcomes.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Discussed qualitatively and as a theme: token-budget management and context-window cost (working memory / context engineering overlap), compression-vs-fidelity trade-offs in latent memory, O(n^2) full-sequence cost vs incremental summarization, I/O/compute burden of real-time memory updates under high-frequency interaction (motivating delayed-consistency strategies like MOOM/LightMem), efficiency gains from autonomous retrieval timing/intent (reducing unnecessary retrieval noise), and frameworks like LightMem targeting lightweight/efficient memory. No single concrete latency/cost number is the focus (it is a survey).
context_budget_and_selection_count: Survey-level: the finite context window is a core motivation; working memory and context engineering manage a bounded token budget via compression, importance-based selection/token pruning, rolling summaries, and OS-style paging (MemGPT main vs external context; MemoryOS/MemOS tiered stores). Selection count ranges from fixed top-K (default) to comprehensive 'retrieve-from-all-stores' (MIRIX) to dynamic/budget-capped policies; the survey critiques forced-top-K and advocates adaptive selection. No single k value is prescribed.
survey_scope_and_axes: Primary organizing axes: the 'Forms-Functions-Dynamics' triangle. FORMS = {Token-level (explicit/discrete; flat 1D / planar 2D / hierarchical 3D), Parametric (internal weight edits & external adapters/LoRA), Latent (KV-cache reuse, generated soft tokens, transformed/compressed hidden states)}. FUNCTIONS = {Factual, Experiential, Working memory}. DYNAMICS = {Formation (extraction), Evolution (consolidation / updating / forgetting), Retrieval (timing & intent / query construction / retrieval strategies / post-retrieval processing)}. Plus Section 2 scope delineation vs LLM memory / RAG / Context Engineering; Section 6 resources (benchmarks Table 8, open-source frameworks Table 9); Section 7 frontiers (retrieval->generation, manual->autonomous, heuristic->RL-driven, multimodal, multi-agent, trustworthiness). Coverage window through early 2026 (v2 revised 2026-01-13). Reference count not explicitly stated in extracted text [uncertain]; bibliography is large (hundreds of entries).
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A as a proposed benchmark, but the survey reports sizes/features for compiled benchmarks in Table 8, e.g., MemBench 53,000 samples (interactive scenarios), LoCoMo 300 samples (conversational memory, multimodal, real), LongMemEval 5 tasks/500 samples (interactive memory), MemoryBank 194 samples, MPR 108,000 samples, PrefEval 3,000, PerLTQA 8,593, StreamBench 9,702 (continuous online learning), MM-Needle ~280,000 (multimodal long-context retrieval), HaluMem 3,467 (memory hallucinations), ALFWorld 3,353 tasks, AgentGym 89 tasks/20,509 samples. It distinguishes simulated vs real environments and factual vs experiential evaluation.
builds_on: Cognitive-science foundations: declarative memory theory (episodic vs semantic; Tulving, Squire) and multicomponent / embedded-processes working-memory models. RAG taxonomy of Mei et al. 2025 (modular / graph / agentic RAG) for the agent-memory-vs-RAG analysis. Foundational systems it taxonomizes: MemGPT, MemoryBank, RET-LLM, Generative Agents, Reflexion/Retroformer, ExpeL, HippoRAG/HippoRAG 2, GraphRAG, AriGraph, Zep, Mem0, A-MEM, AWM, JARVIS-1, Voyager-style skill memory, ReasoningBank, Memento, Memp, MemGen, MEM1, MemAgent.
contrasts_with: Explicitly contrasts agent memory with (1) LLM memory (which agent memory 'almost fully subsumes' - architectural optimizations of representational capacity), (2) RAG (static knowledge access for single-task invocation, evaluated on HotpotQA/2WikiMQA/MuSiQue, vs persistent evolving multi-turn memory), and (3) Context Engineering (transient resource management of the finite context window vs cognitive modeling of a persistent evolving identity). It also positions against traditional long/short-term-memory taxonomies as 'insufficient', and against prior fragmented/loosely-defined agent-memory terminology and earlier memory surveys.
lineage: Surveys group - a late-2025/early-2026 anchor agent-memory survey. It explicitly extends and sharpens the lineage of prior LLM-agent memory surveys (e.g., Zhang et al. 2024 'A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of LLM-based Agents' sources/forms/operations framework) by reorganizing the field around Forms x Functions x Dynamics and by carefully delineating agent memory from RAG and context engineering. It sits alongside and is contemporaneous with other 2026 memory surveys (e.g., 'Rethinking Memory Mechanisms of Foundation Agents', graph-based agent-memory taxonomies, 4W memory taxonomy) and underpins the experience/memory-augmented agent and self-evolving-agent lineage.
